Let \(L_i\) and \(U_i\) denote the lower and upper vertices in column \(i\), where \(0\le i\le 10\).

Because horizontal and diagonal moves can only be made from left to right, the bug can visit each column only once. Thus, after first reaching either vertex in column \(i\), it has exactly three ways to reach a vertex in column \(i+1\).

- From \(L_i\):
  1. \(L_i\to L_{i+1}\) along the lower horizontal edge;
  2. \(L_i\to U_{i+1}\) along the diagonal;
  3. \(L_i\to U_i\to U_{i+1}\), using the vertical edge and then the upper horizontal edge.

- From \(U_i\):
  1. \(U_i\to U_{i+1}\) along the upper horizontal edge;
  2. \(U_i\to L_i\to L_{i+1}\);
  3. \(U_i\to L_i\to U_{i+1}\), using the vertical edge and then the diagonal.

Each extension is unique and uses no previously traversed segment. Therefore, the number of ways to advance through each of the \(10\) squares is \(3\), giving
\[
3^{10}
\]
ways to reach one of the two vertices in column \(10\).

If the bug reaches \(U_{10}\), it is already at \(B\). If it reaches \(L_{10}\), it must use the final vertical edge to reach \(B\), which is uniquely determined. Hence
\[
N=3^{10}=59049.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sqrt N=3^5=\boxed{243}.
\]
